item.title: Fed's Daly: How much tightening and when is no a decision for right now
item.description:
• No doubt of AI-fueled price pressures
  • AI contributing directly only a modest amount to inflation
  • AI having limited impact on labor market
  • We have an inflation problem, but AI is not doing most of the driving
  • There has been repricing in AI valuations, but it’s not the unwinding of interest or enthusiasm
  • That suggests there’s not a risk to growth
  • There is positive momentum for productivity growth
  • A lot of work being done that we might see more productivity growth in next 1-3 years
  • Stable labor market, positive growth and productivity growth, and high inflation
  • Have to focus on bringing inflation down
  • Just because we have to fight inflation problem now doesn’t mean we should ignore potential that productivity growth could be disinflationary
  • Inflation shocks can compound, can’t be complacent
  • Bias is that further tightening will be needed
  • Inflation is bleeding into services
  • Once services inflation rises it’s sticky
  • Tighter financial conditions are most welcome
  • But markets don’t do the work of the Fed; keeping prices stable is the job of the Fed
  • Financial markets are in alignment with where Fed needs to be

Daly is the surprise hawk here and that matters because she’s historically been a reliable dove — when she says her “bias is that further tightening will be needed,” that’s a committee tell, not an outlier. The services language is the sharpest part: inflation “bleeding into services” and “once services inflation rises it’s sticky” is the exact framework the Fed used to justify the 2022-23 campaign, and reviving it signals she sees second-round effects, not just energy passthrough. The direct rebuttal of Bowman’s financial-conditions argument — markets don’t do the Fed’s work — closes off the main dovish off-ramp. Her AI framing cuts hawkish too: productivity optimism means hiking poses “not a risk to growth,” removing the other excuse to pause. Stack this with Logan and the center of gravity is clearly toward more than the 27.7 bps priced this year. Williams-Logan-Daly versus Bowman isn’t a split; it’s a consensus with one dissenter.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US 30-year bond auction tails as demand disappoints for second straight day
item.description:
• High yield 5.441% vs 5.437% WI

  • Tail of 0.4 basis points

  • Bid-to-cover 2.36x vs 2.44x average

  • Dealers awarded 11.39% vs 9.49% average

The US Treasury sold $25 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday in a disappointing auction that adds to signs of softening demand at the long end of the curve.

The auction stopped at 5.441%, a 0.4 basis point tail compared to the 5.437% when-issued yield. That's a deterioration from last month's 0.1 basis point tail and compares unfavourably with the six-auction average of a 0.1 basis point stop-through.

The bid-to-cover ratio fell to 2.36x from 2.54x previously, also below the 2.44x six-auction average.

The breakdown of buyers wasn't particularly encouraging either. Indirect bidders, which include foreign central banks and other institutional investors, took 68.11%, down from 72.32% last month and below the 70.49% average.

Dealers were left holding 11.39%, up sharply from 6.79% in the previous auction. Direct bidders took 20.5%, roughly in line with recent averages.

The results follow Tuesday's soft 10-year auction and suggest that investors remain reluctant to aggressively add duration, even after yields cheapened ahead of the sale.

The good news is that the high yield was well below last month's 5.618%, but that's more a reflection of the broader rally in bonds than stronger underlying demand.

The takeaway is another weak auction, with the higher dealer allocation particularly troubling. It's not a disaster, but it's hardly a vote of confidence in the long end of the Treasury market.

item.title: Gold tumbles $112 as sellers break below the late-October/early-November low
item.description:
Gold is trading sharply lower, down around $112, or 2.82%, at $3875 after reaching a session low near $3852.

The decline in gold is also being reinforced by a higher US dollar and sharply higher Treasury yields. The US 2-year yield is up nearly 14 basis points at 4.86%, while the 10-year yield has climbed nearly 12 basis points to 5.11%. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while higher yields increase the opportunity cost of holding the non-interest-bearing metal. Together, those moves are adding to the selling pressure as gold breaks below key technical support.

The selling has taken the price below the low from late October/early November near $3870, extending the bearish sequence on the 4-hour chart.

The sellers are making a bigger play. The buyers have work to do to take back control.

Failed rallies set the stage.

Earlier this week, buyers had opportunities to shift the technical bias. Monday’s rally moved above the 200-bar moving average on the 4-hour chart, while yesterday’s advance pushed above the 100-bar moving average. Neither break could be sustained.

Those failed breaks matter. The buyers had their chance to build upside momentum, but the inability to hold above the moving averages put the sellers back in control. Those averages now sit near $4027 for the 100-bar and $4090 for the 200-bar, providing overhead resistance.

The old floor becomes a ceiling.

Today’s decline also broke below the swing area between $3942.71 and $3959.37. That area had provided a floor on several occasions going back to July. With the price now below it, the area becomes a key risk and bias-defining ceiling.

Stay below, and the sellers retain firm control. A move back above would ease some of the immediate downside pressure and give buyers a foothold. However, they would still need to reclaim the falling moving averages to strengthen the recovery.

What comes next?

The late-October/early-November low near $3870 is the first nearby barometer. Gold is trading just above that level after bouncing from today’s low, so traders will be watching whether the recovery can hold or whether sellers force the price back below it.

Below today’s $3852 low, the next major downside target comes near $3800, where the lower boundary of the descending channel is currently located. That trend line is moving lower over time.

For traders, the lesson is straightforward: a sharp fall alone does not establish a bottom. Buyers need to reclaim broken levels and hold above them. Until that happens, rallies toward resistance give sellers defined levels to lean against, with $3942–$3959 the key ceiling to watch.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil inventories +4.657 million versus -1.109 million estimate
item.description:
US petroleum inventory data for the week ending November 6:

  • Crude oil inventories: +4.657M barrels vs −1.109M expected. Prior −0.865M.

  • Distillate inventories: +4.071M barrels vs −0.968M expected. Prior −3.565M.

  • Gasoline inventories: +1.799M barrels vs −0.084M expected. Prior −0.222M.

  • Cushing crude inventories: +0.106M barrels. Prior +0.280M.

  • Refinery utilization change: +0.7 percentage point vs +0.4 expected. Prior +1.7 points.

Tuesday’s private inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed builds as well:

  • Crude oil: +9.0M barrels.

  • Gasoline: +4.0M barrels.

  • Distillates: +1.5M barrels.

  • Cushing: +0.182M barrels.

The US Energy Information Administration’s weekly petroleum figures showed unexpected builds across crude oil, gasoline and distillate inventories. Crude stocks increased by 4.657 million barrels against expectations for a 1.109 million-barrel draw—a 5.766 million-barrel upside surprise.

Tuesday’s private data had already flagged broad inventory increases. The EIA crude build was smaller than the API’s 9.0 million-barrel increase, while gasoline also posted a smaller build. However, the EIA distillate increase of 4.071 million barrels was considerably larger than the private estimate of 1.5 million.

Quick analysis: The numbers lean bearish for oil relative to consensus, with inventories rising across all three major categories. However, traders who adjusted expectations after Tuesday’s API report may take some relief from the smaller crude and gasoline builds. The larger distillate build offsets that detail. Weekly trade flows and refinery activity can influence inventories, so the increases alone do not establish weaker demand. Any sustained pressure on energy prices could help headline inflation, but one weekly report has limited implications for Fed policy.

What this report measures: The Energy Information Administration (EIA) Weekly Petroleum Status Report tracks US petroleum inventories, refinery activity, production and trade flows. The American Petroleum Institute publishes a separate private survey ahead of the government report; differences in survey coverage and methodology mean the figures can diverge. Traders watch unexpected builds or draws for clues about supply, demand and oil prices.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro falls to the lowest since April 2025
item.description:
The euro has cut through modest support at the May 2025 low and is now at the worst levels since April of last year.

The pressure is coming from the US dollar side of the equation as Treasury yields rise once again today. Fed hawk Beth Hammack pushed back against the idea of a 50 basis point rate hike but there is an increasing chorus at the Fed that rates need to rise to 'restrictive' levels and that they're currently still in accommodative territory.

The takeaway is that two hikes won't be enough and now the market is pricing in 85 bps of hikes in the year ahead. In addition, the market is wondering what they have seen to make them so alarmed. Some of that likely came through the latest CPI report, which saw a broadening of inflation pressures. 

In terms of today's price action, US 2-year yields rose 12 bps today to 4.85%. That's up from 4.44% on November 6 and we're now within striking distance of the September highs.

Meanwhile, the eurozone appears closer to the end of the rate hiking cycle with the market pricing in about 50 basis points in the year ahead. 

Another important part of the dynamic is AI. Money is flooding into the US for AI investment opportunities and we're seeing an uptick in AI trades. Today, CNBC reported that OpenAI raised $15 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation. That's a good sign for Anthropic ahead of next week's IPO. The valuation range is said to be $1.25-1.75 trillion, and they're widely seen as more-valuable than OpenAI.

If there's a strong IPO, we could see an ebb in worries about neoclouds and AI capex in general. We saw some good news this week as CoreWeave jumped on earnings (though it has given back some today). Memory names have also rebounded.

Ultimately, this trade will come down to economic momentum and the market isn't finding reasons to bet on Europe at the moment.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Goolsbee: Inflation has been well-above target
item.description:
• AI investment looks like a form of stimulus
  • Worth being 'sober minded' about inflation an Fed response
  • Fed is failing on the inflation side of its mandate
  • Does not want to prejudice what happens with monetary policy
  • Plenty of room for the Fed to discuss policy options

The market is pricing in 87 bps of hikes in the year ahead.

That first line is the one that matters. Stimulus is a demand word. For two years the Fed’s framing on AI was about supply: productivity, capacity, a disinflationary tailwind somewhere down the road. Goolsbee is now describing it the way you’d describe a fiscal package.

It’s an extension of what he’s been saying for a month. In October he said inflation was starting to feel like aggregate overheating, with data center costs spilling into the broader economy. On Monday he said the build-out increasingly resembled traditional demand overheating, the kind central banks need to hit aggressively up front.

Then came Tuesday’s CPI. Headline prices rose 0.4% in October and core rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Waller said he would consider voting for 50 bps in December and Logan wants at least two more hikes.

Remember who this is. Goolsbee was among the most reliable doves on the committee through the cutting cycle. When he’s calling capex stimulus, the debate at the Fed is no longer whether to hike. It’s how fast.

The market is there already. There are 87 bps of hikes priced for the year ahead, which is three hikes and a coin flip on a fourth from the current 3.75-4.00%. December is fully priced, with about a 13% chance of 50 bps. The 10-year is back above 5% and the dollar hit a 19-month high this week.

‘Sober minded’ is the tell on pace. That’s not the language of someone itching for 50. It’s 25 bps and keep going.

Here’s the problem with hiking against a capex boom: hyperscalers aren’t rate sensitive. Housing is, and so is the consumer. The Fed can lean on the parts of the economy that aren’t overheating to offset the part that is, and that’s an ugly trade.

The other way this cools is that credit markets do the work for them. Watch AI-linked debt as closely as the dots.

Goolsbee votes in 2027.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The US dollar moves higher as Treasury yields extend their gains
item.description:
The US dollar is moving higher as rising Treasury yields give buyers another push. The 2-year yield is up nearly 11 basis points at 4.837%, while the 10-year yield is up 7.7 basis points at 5.066%. The 10 year yield bottomed last week at 4.814%.

What does not quite line up is the change in Fed policy expectations for December. The probability of a 50-basis-point hike from the Fed at the December meeting has slipped to about 6.5% from nearly 14% yesterday. In isolation, that should take some pressure off the dollar. So far, however, the rise in yields is carrying more weight, and dollar buyers remain in control.

EURUSD technicals.

The EURUSD has extended to a new low of 1.1053, breaking below both the earlier session low at 1.1066 and the May 2025 low at 1.1060. Those broken levels now provide the first close resistance. Staying below them would keep sellers firmly in control.

For traders looking for further downside, the former October floor between 1.1103 and 1.1112 provides a more conservative risk area. Sellers would not want to see the price move back above that zone. A recovery through it would weaken the bearish bias and raise questions about the break lower.

GBPUSD Technicals.

The GBPUSD has moved away from the October 28 low near 1.32729 and gathered additional downside momentum after breaking below the earlier session low near 1.3249.

That move has taken the pair toward the middle of the broader range that contained most of the price action from mid-September to mid-October, between 1.3171 and 1.3310. The lower boundary at 1.3171 is now the next key downside target.

On the topside, the broken 1.3249 level is the first hurdle, followed by more important resistance near 1.32729. Staying below that latter level keeps the sellers in control. Move back above it, and the downside momentum starts to lose some traction.

USDCAD Technicals.

The USDCAD moved lower earlier in the session, but buyers stepped in ahead of the swing level at 1.42205. The low reached 1.4225 before the pair rotated back higher with the broader dollar buying.

The subsequent rally has taken the price to a new session high at 1.4270. There is limited resistance before the October swing highs between 1.42918 and 1.42986. That area is the next key upside target.

Move above that zone and stay above it, and the door opens for further upside momentum. If sellers lean against those highs, a rotation lower would keep the resistance area in play. On the downside, the 1.42205–1.4225 area now defines the support that buyers successfully defended today.

AUDUSD Technicals

The AUDUSD has extended to a new low at 0.6799, with today’s decline taking the price below a key swing area between 0.6832 and 0.6863. That zone had provided a floor going back to mid-January. With the break lower, the former floor now becomes a ceiling and a key risk area for sellers.

Adding to the importance of that zone is the 50% midpoint of the move up from the November 2025 low to the early May high. That level comes in at 0.68499, within the swing area. Today’s move below—and away from—that midpoint strengthens the bearish bias.

As long as the price remains below 0.6832–0.6863, sellers remain in control. Buyers would need to reclaim that area to question the break lower and shift the bias back in their favor.

On the downside, the next target comes in at 0.67658, followed by the 61.8% retracement at 0.6749. Those are the next hurdles for sellers as they look to extend the downside momentum.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: As market digest the Nvidia fallout, what has the fallout meant for the Nasdaq composite/Nasdaq 100 indices?
item.description:
Shares of Nvidia bounced after testing the technical target area between $146.50 and $151.84. The low reached $148.80, putting the price within the support zone outlined in the earlier video.

Buyers leaned against that area and pushed the price higher. But what has the fallout meant for the broader technology indices, including the NASDAQ composite and NASDAQ 100?

Both indices have bounced near important technical support. However, the buyers still have work to do before they can claim more control.

NASDAQ composite: Buyers lean against a key support area

The NASDAQ composite moved below its 200 day moving average at 25,129.88, but found buyers ahead of the 38.2% retracement of the move up from the April low at 25,036.33.

The session low reached 25,068.28, putting it between those two technical levels. Buyers leaned against that support area and pushed the index back above its 200 day moving average, with the rebound reaching a high of 25,401.16.

That gives buyers something to build on. The 200 day moving average at 25,129.88 now becomes a close risk barometer. Staying above it would keep the recovery moving in the right direction.

However, the next important upside hurdle is the falling 100 hour moving average at 25,587.98. If the buyers are to take more control, they need to get above that moving average and stay above it. A sustained break would open the door for a move toward the next target at 25,831.74.

Conversely, a move back below the 200 day moving average would weaken the recovery. A further break below the 38.2% retracement at 25,036.33 would give sellers more control and open the door for additional downside momentum.

The next key downside target would be the 50% midpoint at 24,206.50. Recall that the decline earlier this month stalled just ahead of that level.

The support area has attracted buyers. Now they need to show they can hold the recovery and break resistance.

NASDAQ 100: A failed break gives buyers another chance

The NASDAQ 100 moved below its 38.2% retracement at 28,108.03 and its 200 day moving average at 28,028.41. However, sellers could not sustain momentum below the moving average.

The index has since rebounded to around 28,158, putting it back above both technical levels. That failed break gives buyers another chance, with the reclaimed support area now acting as a close risk barometer.

On the topside, the falling 100 hour moving average at 28,460.25 remains the next key hurdle. Getting above—and staying above—that level would strengthen the buyers’ position and put the swing area between 28,822 and 28,953 in play.

Conversely, a move back below 28,108.03 and then 28,028.41 would weaken the recovery and give sellers another opportunity to extend the decline. The next key downside target would be the 50% midpoint of the move up from the end of March low at 27,103.

The trading lesson: A bounce is the first step

Holding support helps define risk. It does not, by itself, establish that the trend has turned.

For the NASDAQ composite, buyers found support between the 38.2% retracement and the 200 day moving average before reclaiming the moving average. For the NASDAQ 100, the break below its 200 day moving average failed to attract sustained selling.

Those reactions matter. They give traders reference points to lean against and measure whether the buyers can remain in the game.

The next test is overhead. Both indices need to get above their falling 100 hour moving averages and stay above them to strengthen the bullish bias. If the support levels give way first, the sellers regain control.

In the video above, I take a look at both broader indices and provide an updated look at Nvidia as its volatile trading continues.

Be aware. Be prepared.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October existing home sales 3.75m vs 3.85m expected
item.description:
• Prior was 3.99m (revised to 3.97m)
  • Sales -5.5% vs +1.5% prior (revised to +1.0%)
  • Inventory at 5.1 months
  • Median price $416,700, up 0.4% y/y

The US housing market is in a deep slump and there is no help coming from the Fed. At some point it will turn but we're not there yet.

For background, the National Association of Realtors publishes its existing home sales report monthly at 10 am ET, usually in the third or fourth week of the following month. Existing homes make up roughly 90% of US home sales, so the report is the broadest monthly read on housing market activity.

The headline figure is the seasonally adjusted annualized rate of sales, covering single-family homes, townhomes, condominiums and co-ops. Because the data count closed transactions, they reflect contracts signed one to two months earlier. NAR’s pending home sales index, released later each month, tracks contract signings and gives an earlier signal of where closings are headed.

The report also includes the median existing-home price, which isn’t seasonally adjusted and is usually compared with the same month a year earlier. Because it’s a median, it can be skewed by changes in the mix of homes selling, such as more high-end sales in a given month. Repeat-sales measures like Case-Shiller give a cleaner read on price trends.

Inventory is one of the most closely watched details. NAR reports the number of homes for sale and months’ supply, the time it would take to sell current inventory at the current sales pace. Around six months is generally considered a balanced market. The report also tracks first-time buyers’ share of sales, all-cash purchases, investor activity and days on market.

Existing home sales rarely move broader markets. Their value is in showing how mortgage rates and affordability are affecting housing turnover. Sales have been held down in recent years by the lock-in effect, with homeowners reluctant to give up low-rate mortgages, which has kept inventory tight and prices elevated despite weak volumes.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Now that all the Nvidia/Jensen Huang news is out, what next for traders in Nvidia?
item.description:
With the news of Jensen Huang’s departure and Nvidia’s leadership transition now out, the focus for traders shifts to the next question: What happens from here?

In the video above, I look at that question from a technical perspective. What levels matter for buyers and sellers? Why do they matter? And what does the price need to do to signal a rebound or open the door for more selling?

Traders need to remember that news changes all the time. We never know every development that will influence the price. My guess is that very few traders had Huang resigning as CEO and a board member on their bingo card—or included that possibility in their risk assessment. But it happened.

That uncertainty is why I focus on price action and technical tools. We cannot anticipate every headline, but we can identify when the price breaks a key level and use that break to define our bias and risk.

For Nvidia, the move below its 200 day moving average, currently at $204.31, was an important technical warning. Staying below that level strengthened the bearish bias, and the last three trading days have brought additional selling pressure. The full story was still unfolding, but the price was already moving lower.

Now that the leadership announcement is public, some traders may see an opportunity to buy the dip. However, a lower price alone does not define a trade. Buyers still need to ask: Where am I wrong? What support am I leaning against? And what resistance must the price reclaim to show that buyers are taking back control?

Those are the questions I address in the video above. The technical levels provide a roadmap for both sides of the market. They help define where a rebound can gain traction, where sellers may lean against resistance, and where another break could trigger more downside momentum.

The news provides the catalyst. The price action helps define the bias, the risk and the next targets.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin breaks key support. What can traders learn from the move?
item.description:
Bitcoin sellers are making a bigger play today with the price moving below its 200 day moving average at $73,086 and the 50% retracement of the recent trend move higher from the July 1 low which comes in at $72,554 (see the chart below). The current price is trading at $72,216. Those breaks are key for traders, and because of them, they will now require buyers to reclaim those broken levels to take some of the selling pressure off, and to take back some control from the sellers.

The educational lesson is how those technical levels help traders make decisions. Where are buyers making a stand? What happens when that support breaks? What would tell sellers that the break is failing?

Those questions turn a chart into a trading plan.

Support gives buyers a place to lean.

A key moving average or retracement (outlined in the chart above) gives buyers a reference point. Buyers can lean against support with the expectation that the level will hold. If it does, they have an opportunity to participate in a rebound with relatively close risk. Yesterday the price fell below the 200 day moving average, but could not get below the 50% retracement level. The price rebounded back higher. The rebound to the upside ended up finding willing sellers against the low of the swing area between $74,925 and $76,082. The high price got withing $300 of that level, but the rally stalled. The inability to get back into the old floor area (the floor became the ceiling), gave the sellers the go-ahead to push the downside - and they did.

So although there was support near the 200 day and the 50% retracement yesterday, traders need to understand that support does not come with a guarantee. Those levels are still in play.  They also need to understand that there are benchmarks that any corrective move has to reach to turn the bias around. That was the old floor (now ceiling). 

Today, when the price breaks below and stays below the 200 day and the 50% retracement, the reason for buying against that level weakens. Buyers need to recognize that change. A trade entered with close risk loses that advantage if the trader keeps moving the exit farther away.

That is the first lesson: identify what would prove the trade wrong before entering it.

Broken support becomes a barometer.

Today, the 200 day and the 50% have been broken.  With Bitcoin below both technical references, the 200 day moving average and 50% retracement become overhead barometers and risk defining levels.

If a rebound stalls against those levels, sellers retain the technical advantage. Buyers may be pushing the price higher, but they still need to get through the resistance created by the break.

If the price moves back above both levels and stays above, the bearish break becomes less convincing. Sellers would need to respect the possibility of a failed break and a further recovery.

The distinction is important. Trading below a level gives one message. Breaking below and then quickly recovering gives another.

A break needs follow-through.

A move through support is the first step. What happens afterward helps determine the quality of the break.

Can sellers keep the price below the broken levels? Do rebounds attract selling? Can the price extend toward the next downside target?

If those things happen, sellers strengthen their control. If downside momentum stalls and buyers reclaim the broken levels, the technical picture changes.

Traders do not have to predict that outcome in advance. They need to recognize which outcome is developing and manage their risk accordingly.

Define the risk. Then follow the price.

The approach I discuss in my book, Attacking Currency Trends, centers on using technical tools to identify opportunities and define risk. That same discipline can be applied to Bitcoin.

For this setup, the process is straightforward:

  • Bias: Sellers have the technical advantage while the price remains below the broken support levels.

  • Risk: A sustained recovery above those levels would weaken the bearish case.

  • Targets: Further downside progress requires sellers to break—and stay below—the next support levels.

Knowing the direction you want to trade is only part of the job. Knowing where that trade stops making sense is just as important.

For Bitcoin, the sellers have made their move. The next test is whether they can keep control below the broken support. Buyers have their assignment too: reclaim those levels and stay above them.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang ousted as CEO of Nvidia
item.description:
This was the mother of all hit jobs. The timing, everything. My suspicion is that he wasn't cracking down hard enough on China sales, or turning a blind eye and that the China hawks orchestrated his downfall.

CFO Colette Kress will take over leadership on an interim basis while they search for a permanent CEO. 

Earnings will take place on November 17, as previously scheduled.

The WSJ reported early that the board was preparing to oust Huang so this isn't entirely surprising. Shares were down 9% before the announcement and have fallen further, now down around 11%.

Here is the press release:

NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition

November 12, 2026
  • Jensen Huang Resigns
  • Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
  • Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

item.title: Why markets sometimes ignore economic data
item.description:
Key economic releases are among the most closely watched events in financial markets. Inflation figures, employment reports, business surveys and so on can all influence expectations for monetary policy and the macroeconomic outlook. Yet, markets do not always react to the data in the same way. 

The key thing to understand is that financial markets are forward-looking. Asset prices reflect expectations about future economic conditions, central bank decisions and so on. It's never about the present conditions. The market reaction to an economic release depends on whether it changes the underlying expectations.

Not every economic release carries the same importance. For example, a stronger than expected employment report might initially push bond yields higher. However, if inflation is simultaneously declining and the central bank is becoming more concerned about missing the inflation target, the employment surprise might not be enough to change expectations for interest rates.

The opposite can also happen. A relatively small inflation surprise could have a significant impact if markets think that it's going to change the central bank's next move.

Central banks generally determine which data matters most

Policymakers monitor a wide range of economic indicators, but the relative importance of each variable changes depending on the economic context. When inflation is the main for a central bank concern, markets become very sensitive to inflation data like CPI, PPI, wage growth and so on. When the focus shifts to the labour market, jobs data like NFP, jobless claims and so on become more important.

So, you can see that the importance changes based on the economic context and central bank's focus. For example, if the Federal Reserve is worried about persistent inflation and has signalled that further monetary tightening might be necessary, an unexpectedly strong inflation report could trigger a significant hawkish repricing. A weaker consumer confidence report might have little to no impact because it does not address the Fed's immediate concern.

This is why central bank's communication matters so much for markets. Policymakers often indicate which economic variables they are monitoring most closely. Traders then adjust their focus accordingly, making certain releases more market-moving than others.

Positioning also matters

Market positioning can also determine how prices react to economic data. If traders already expect a particular outcome, a report confirming that expectation may trigger little to no reaction at all. This is what happened during the first months with the CPI reports as markets already expected inflation to jump due to the spike in energy prices caused by the US-Iran war. 

This can become even more important when positioning get overcrowded. If traders are heavily positioned for a certain outcome and conditions change, the repricing of expectations can lead to big market moves as traders rush to adjust their positions. 

A good example is tomorrow's US PPI release. The report comes after two key developments have already significantly shifted market expectations for monetary policy.

First, Fed's Waller delivered some very hawkish remarks, supporting a December rate hike and raising the possibility of a larger increase if inflation data surprised to the upside. Then, the US CPI report came in hotter than expected, sealing the case for a rate hike in December and raising the chances of a 50 bps move.

This means that tomorrow's PPI report is unlikely to trigger a significant market reaction because it wouldn't change the current expectations, even if the data come in above expectations. Most of the hawkish repricing has already taken place, leaving little room for further repricing. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: US weekly initial jobless claims 200K vs 195K expected
item.description:
• Prior was 189K
  • Four week average vs 194.75K prior
  • Continuing claims vs 1710K expected

The US Department of Labor publishes its weekly unemployment insurance claims report every Thursday at 8:30 am ET, or Wednesday when a holiday falls later in the week. It’s the most timely official read on the US labor market, covering the week that ended just five days earlier.

The headline figure is initial jobless claims, the number of people filing for unemployment benefits for the first time. It’s a direct gauge of layoffs. Because the weekly data are noisy, markets also watch the four-week moving average to gauge the trend.

The report also includes continuing claims, the number of people still receiving benefits after their initial filing, which lags initial claims by a week. While initial claims track layoffs, continuing claims show how hard it is for people out of work to find new jobs. A steady rise in continuing claims alongside low initial claims has often signaled a “low-hire, low-fire” labor market where workers aren’t being let go but are struggling to get rehired.

Claims tend to get extra attention during the week that includes the 12th of the month, which is the survey reference week for the monthly nonfarm payrolls report, giving an early hint at the jobs data.

Seasonal adjustment is a persistent challenge. Holidays, summer auto plant retooling, school calendars, hurricanes and strikes can distort the numbers, as can surges in fraudulent filings in individual states. The report includes unadjusted state-level data and separate figures for federal employees, which can matter during government layoffs or shutdowns.

Because claims are released weekly and few other labor indicators are as current, a sustained break higher is one of the clearest early warning signs of a weakening economy.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Yields climb as Nvidia slides below key support. USD mixed.

Higher U.S. yields have not translated into a uniform dollar advance. That makes the individual currency charts important. Traders still need to see where buyers can hold support and where sellers can keep a lid on rallies.

The trade figures were less encouraging. The goods deficit widened to £22.3 billion versus £19.2 billion expected and £19.6 billion previously.

GBPUSD, USDCHF and USDCAD have completed the smallest portions of their normal month long average ranges. AUDUSD has traveled the furthest relative to its average.

There is room for an extension in most pairs if the data or a technical break gives traders a reason to act. The average is a reference point, however. It does not require the market to travel a particular distance.

The trading lesson.

Nvidia provides a practical example of why a swing area matters. A floor marks an area where buyers previously showed up. If the price opens below it, those buyers have to prove they can reclaim it.

The headline creates the movement. The price action around the technical level helps us define the trade and limit the risk.

item.title: How IPOs work: The process of bringing a company to the stock market
item.description:
An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is the process through which a privately held company offers its shares to the public for the first time and becomes listed on a stock exchange. An IPO allows a company to raise capital from a broader pool of investors while giving the public an opportunity to participate in its growth.

Before going public, ownership is generally concentrated among founders, employees, venture capital funds and other private investors. An IPO changes this by creating a public market where institutional and retail investors can buy and sell shares.

Companies go public to raise capital for expansion, research, acquisitions or debt reduction. An IPO can also provide liquidity to existing shareholders, increase the company's visibility and make it easier to use publicly traded shares for acquisitions or employee compensation.

How does an IPO work?

The IPO process usually begins with the company appointing investment banks, known as underwriters, to manage the offering. These banks help determine the company's valuation, structure the transaction, prepare the regulatory documentation and market the shares to potential investors.

In the US, companies generally file a registration statement called Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This document provides detailed information about the company's business model, financial performance, risks, management and intended use of the proceeds. It is one of the most important documents investors examine before participating in an IPO.

The company and its underwriters then establish an indicative price range based on financial performance, growth prospects, comparable listed companies and expected investor demand. During the roadshow, management presents the business to institutional investors to gauge interest and determine how much they are willing to pay.

Once demand has been assessed, the final IPO price is established and shares are allocated to investors. The stock then begins trading on the selected exchange, where its price is determined by supply and demand.

Primary vs. secondary shares

An important distinction is whether the shares offered during an IPO are newly issued or sold by existing shareholders. The primary shares are newly issued by the company, meaning the proceeds go directly to the business and provide fresh capital for investments and operations.

The secondary shares are existing shares sold by current shareholders, such as founders, employees or venture capital funds. In this case, the proceeds go to the selling shareholders rather than the company.

IPO stocks usually experience significant price swings during their first trading sessions because the market is still establishing a fair value. An important factor is the lock-up period. Existing shareholders are often restricted from selling their shares for a predetermined period following the IPO. When these restrictions expire, earlier investors can sell their shares, often increasing selling pressure. This is one of the main reasons behind the usual underperformance of IPO stocks over the short-term.

Broader market conditions generally matter more than idiosyncratic fundamentals. Strong risk appetite and favourable financial conditions generally support demand for new listings, while periods of uncertainty and tighter monetary policy can make investors more cautious.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: How could Japan shake up the global markets?
item.description:
How could Japan shake up the global markets?

Minutes from the Bank of Japan’s October meeting point to another rate hike in December, and it’s easy to see why.

The weak yen and rising energy costs driven by Middle East tensions have pushed core inflation to 2.1% year over year in September, its highest level since early 2026 and above the BOJ’s 2% target, while the measure excluding food and energy climbed to 2.4%. Higher oil pricesadd to these inflationary pressures, particularly because Japan relies heavily on energy imports. This also makes oil prices an important factor to watch when assessing the BOJ’s next policy move.

As for why the BOJ is holding back, even though the conditions for a hike are already in place, a tighter policy could help bring inflation under control and ease pressure on the yen, but it would also make borrowing more expensive, potentially cooling business activity and investment.

Another reason is Japan’s massive government debt, which exceeds 200% of GDP. Rather than paying it off, the government keeps rolling over maturing bonds by issuing new ones, while continuing to pay interest on its debt.

This means that higher rates would make that debt increasingly expensive to service, putting even more pressure on public finances and raising concerns about long-term debt sustainability. 

Currency intervention could also help ease some of this pressure. By selling US dollars and buying yen, Japan’s authorities can support the currency and curb imported inflation. Such intervention could also trigger a sharp move lower in USD/JPY, depending on its scale and how markets interpret the authorities’ intentions. The yen they receive can then be withdrawn from circulation, reducing liquidity in the economy.

The catch is that Japan’s reserves, while substantial, are not unlimited. And a large part of them is held in US Treasuries.

If Japan starts selling those bonds to support the yen rather than hiking rates, Treasury yields could climb, putting pressure on global markets, particularly riskier assets. After all, why take risks in stocks when you can earn a relatively safe 5% on government bonds?

A Fed rate cut could offer relief to both US and Japanese markets by making the yen carry trade less attractive, but with inflation still running hot and the labor market holding up, that looks unlikely for now. 

On the other hand, if the Fed does move in the opposite directionto BOJ and the carry trade unwinds, it could create another problem: investors who borrowed yen to buy foreign assets may be forced to sell them to repay their loans. This could trigger a repeat of the 2024 sell-off across markets. 

 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Why falling oil prices might not deliver the inflation relief everyone expects
item.description:
Oil prices are starting to fall again, so surely that must mean our cost-of-living problems should be disappearing too, right? Well, if only the economics behind that were so straightforward and cooperative.

WTI crude has dropped back to just below $86 today amid hopes of easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. That is welcome news for households especially after the energy shock this year and I can understand why markets are getting excited as well.

But before popping the champagne, this is something worth remembering. Cheaper oil doesn't necessarily mean cheaper living.

Sure, lower oil prices should eventually bring some relief to let's say the gasoline pump. That means transportation and shipping costs could also ease, affording businesses a little bit more breathing room.

But here's something to think about. When was the last time that your rent, insurance bill or favourite restaurant actually became cheaper? Dum, dum, dum. Exactly. And this is precisely where the inflation story gets a little more complicated beyond just falling oil prices.

Just take a look at the chart above. Since January 2020, gasoline prices have jumped by nearly 68% while food and shelter costs have risen by around 35% and 34% respectively in the US. Meanwhile, overall consumer prices have increased by roughly 31%.

Now, here's the interesting bit. Nominal wages have also risen by nearly 34% during the same period, slightly outpacing overall inflation. On paper, that suggests the average worker should be a little better off, no? Well, not quite.

The fact of the matter is that we don't all spend our money the same way. If you're spending a bigger chunk of your income on things like groceries, rent and gasoline, then those price increases can still sting. And a cheaper tank of gasoline today isn't going to magically reverse years of higher living costs.

Anyway, let's put aside the numbers and focus on what's really important here. At the end of the day, inflation coming down doesn't mean prices are coming down. It simply means that prices are still rising, just more slowly.

So even if gasoline prices are to fall today, that doesn't undo years of increases in housing, food, healthcare and other essential expenses. And then there's another twist to all of this too. Cheaper fuel leaves consumers with more money to spend elsewhere, potentially supporting demand and keeping some price pressures alive.

So, what does all this mean for the Fed?

I think it's relatively straightforward. Falling oil prices can help to ease the pressure showing up on headline inflation. However, policymakers need to see broader improvements in underlying price pressures before they can feel comfortable changing course.

With that in mind, I would argue that markets ought to pay more attention to things like core services inflation, wage growth, and Treasury yields as compared to watching out for the next $5 or $10 drop in oil prices.

If the next inflation reports show genuine signs of cooling beyond energy, only then markets might have reason to rethink the Fed's policy outlook. But if services inflation stays stubborn, then cheaper oil on its own probably won't be able to move the needle much.

That's sort of the irony of it all now, isn't it? Oil prices might be falling again but the inflation problem isn't necessarily going to follow in that same direction.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: India October CPI inflation rises to 6.09%, food inflation accelerates to 8.94%
item.description:
• India CPI Y/Y 6.09% vs 5.93% expected
  • Prior 5.54%
  • Full report

India's CPI rose to 6.09% y/y in October, according to provisional data, pointing to increased price pressures in the economy. The headline inflation rate was higher in rural areas, where prices increased by 6.63% y/y, compared with 5.41% in urban areas.

Food inflation was a big standout, with the Consumer Food Price Index rising 8.94% y/y in October. Food price increases were relatively broad-based across the country, with rural food inflation reaching 9.09% and urban food inflation standing at 8.68%.

The figures highlight the significant contribution of food prices to India's inflationary pressures, with food inflation running well above the headline CPI rate. Overall, the October report points to a challenging inflation environment for the Reserve Bank of India. Given the acceleration in inflation, the market is pricing in a 69% chance of a 25 bps hike at the next RBI meeting, with 31% probabilitiy of a larger 50 bps move. 

The US-Iran war has been a major contributor of inflation through higher crude oil prices, increasing India's import bill and raising transportation, energy and agricultural production costs.

As a major oil importer, India is particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the Middle East. Higher energy and fertiliser costs gradually feed into consumer prices, while a weaker rupee also makes imports more expensive.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil is caught between hopes of de-escalation and concerns of further escalation. What's next?
item.description:
Crude oil has been consolidating around recent lows as the US-Iran uncertainty keeps traders guessing on the next move.

The US-Iran conflict remains the main driver of course, with diplomatic efforts showing some signs of progress but no concrete breakthrough yet.

Oil prices dipped yesterday after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US Vice President Vance was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official in an effort to end the war.

However, significant mistrust remains, with Iranian officials accusing Washington of preparing further military strikes or tighter economic pressure. Iran has also continued to issue warnings of retaliation against US military bases and reportedly targeted ship navigation systems near the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, the US military says its blockade has prevented Iran from exporting oil, while US forces are working to keep the Strait open to commercial shipping. The conflicting signals leave the outlook highly uncertain, with oil prices remaining sensitive to any developments that could either pave the way for de-escalation or trigger another escalation.

It goes without saying that a concrete breakthrough would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly. But an escalation, on the other hand, could trigger another rally on a rising risk premium, although there’s also a chance that it could be short-lived if Trump launches limited strikes just to save face before exiting the war.

 

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil(CFD contract) is consolidating around the key 87.00 handle. The choppy price action amid the US-Iran uncertainty makes it hard for both sides to pick a direction. The buyers will want to see the price rising above the 87.00 handle to start positioning into new highs, while the sellers will continue to pile in for new lows below the 87.00 level.

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, there’s not much we can glean from this timeframe given the choppy price action around the 87.00 level, so we need to zoom in to see some more details.

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish structure. We can expect the sellers to continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 80.00 handle next. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 110.00 resistance, with the 92.50 level as the first target. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. Tomorrow, we conclude the week with the US PPI data. The focus will remain on US-Iran developments.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
